Range: $(0,\infty)$.

content.prompt: By finding expressions for the LHS and RHS, show that these are true for $f(x)=x^2$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=f(4x)\\&=(4x)^2\\&=16x^2\\\text{RHS}&=16f(x)\\&=16x^2\end{aligned}$$
Thus LHS = RHS.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=f(xy)\\&=(xy)^2\\&=x^2y^2\\\text{RHS}&=f(x)f(y)\\&=x^2y^2\end{aligned}$$
Thus LHS = RHS.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=f\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)\\&=\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^2\\&=\frac{x^2}{y^2}\\\text{RHS}&=\frac{f(x)}{f(y)}\\&=\frac{x^2}{y^2}\end{aligned}$$
Thus LHS = RHS for $y\ne0$.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=f(x^2)\\&=(x^2)^2\\&=x^4\\\text{RHS}&=(f(x))^2\\&=(x^2)^2\\&=x^4\end{aligned}$$
Thus LHS = RHS.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=f(x+y)+f(x-y)\\&=(x+y)^2+(x-y)^2\\&=x^2+2xy+y^2+x^2-2xy+y^2\\&=2x^2+2y^2\\\text{RHS}&=2(f(x)+f(y))\\&=2(x^2+y^2)\\&=2x^2+2y^2\end{aligned}$$
Thus LHS = RHS.
